newsitem.title: CANADA: Half to 80 pct of Ontario wheat to grade as feed.
newsitem.headline: Half to 80 pct of Ontario wheat to grade as feed.

text.p: Fifty to 80 percent of Ontario's main export milling wheat crop may be unfit for human consumption because of fusarium head blight, an Ontario Wheat Producers' Marketing Board official told Reuters.
"Normally, we have five to 10 percent grading as feed wheat. This year, we could have 80 percent of our production as feed," OWPMB secretary manager, William McClounie said.
The single-desk selling agency orginially forecast output at 1.1 million tonnes but reduced it to 680,000 mainly due to an outbreak of fusarium head blight, McClounie said.
Fusarium is brought on by prolonged rain during heading.
The fungus can produce vomitoxin which, in low levels, are tolerable but in high levels can cause nausea.

"Producers have registered their farm storage with us as grade number two (milling wheat) and we have a sneaking suspicion that it's probably feed wheat. They think it's a two but it's probably feed," McClounie said.
At least 350,000 tonnes, or 51 percent of total output, was expected to grade as wheat fit only to feed to animals.
Two thirds of Ontario's winter wheat crop is usually exported to the United States and overseas for milling.
Fusarium headblight was found in two percent of western Canada's milling wheat crop at this point in the fall harvest, the Canadian Grain Commission said.
The level of infection on the Prairies, however, did not appear as severe as in Ontario, with most western fusarium samples graded down to number two milling wheat, the CGC said.
